doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: What angers him; spirituality and the dignity of the musicians
summary: Harper is angered by inhumanity, calls himself spiritual, and says his mentors were dignified gentlemen.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Okay. This might be a tough question, but what kind of things make you angry, either musically or just in life?

I would still say pretty much the same things is people not being human. And that covers a whole lot. I mean when you look at, like be it war, racism, senseless killings, all of it. Because it’s hurtful and it angers you — because we look at all the technology that we have nowadays, the things that we can do — you know talk to somebody from around the world via the computer or send an instant message. You look at all this wonderful technology and we still can’t get along? I mean that to me is always my bug. All the things that we’ve come up with and helped to create, but we can’t treat each other fairly. So that will always anger me, be it whatever it is, race relations, just not wanting to treat other human beings with adequate due respect. I think this should anger everybody.
Are you a spiritual — do you think of yourself as a spiritual person?

Oh very much so. Very much so. And I do believe, I always tell a lot of my students for this music to be approached right and properly you really have to be. I think the majority of those guys who played the music that I knew were. Those guys that I named to you

that I was close with or I worked with were. A lot of times they may not have worn it on their sleeves, but if you got to know them, okay, how they conducted themselves, you knew that there was something underlying in there that was intact. You know, Billy Taylor, Max Roach, Billy Higgins, Jackie McLean, Abdullah Ibrahim. All those guys that I spent time with that had a big influence on me, you know Betty, you knew that there was some things intact. And it had to be for them to be the kind of people that they were. And that was the other beautiful thing about jazz for me too is the way the musicians were. And I think that’s something that’s missing in our society that we need is that all the musicians that I saw, they were so dignified. I mean they were gentlemen.
The Joe Wilders of the world.

Right. It’s like polished. As far as you know, they might not have had two nickels. You know what I mean? But you know they were still dignified. It was something in their intent. It was something that they were trying to say. It was a message in all of it.
